U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years as Outbreaks Spread Across the Country


The United States has lost its measles elimination status, marking a major setback for public health after more than a quarter-century of progress against the highly contagious disease.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional arm of the World Health Organization, determined that measles has been spreading continuously in the country for more than 12 months. The decision ends a status the U.S. first achieved in 2000.

The numbers are raising serious concerns. Approximately 7,700 measles infections and 13 deaths have been reported in the United States since 2025. More than 5,000 cases have been recorded in 2026 alone, according to reports citing public health data.

The resurgence has been linked to declining vaccination rates, growing vaccine hesitancy and outbreaks in several states, including Texas, Utah and Arizona.

Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases. Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide approximately 97% protection, while public health experts generally recommend vaccination coverage of around 95% to prevent sustained community transmission.

The consequences are particularly concerning for infants who are too young to receive their first dose, people with weakened immune systems and those who remain unvaccinated.

Health experts say restoring the country’s measles-free status will require stronger vaccination campaigns, improved disease surveillance and sustained efforts to stop transmission.

For a country that once considered measles elimination a major public health achievement, the latest development is a sobering reminder that decades of progress can be reversed.

The Draft Has an Age Discount

Gadi Eisenkot’s proposed ultra-Orthodox draft deal offers a clean slate to men who have avoided service. Those 26 and older would get a full exemption.

Younger men would have several months to settle their status. Some aged 18 to 20 could defer service for up to two years before enlisting. 

Those aged 21 to 25 could take a shortened training course and join the reserves, guarding border communities to relieve existing reservists. Those who refuse would face personal sanctions.

An annual exemption would remain for exceptional religious scholars who pass tests, capped at 3% of the national recruitment cohort, or about 2,500 men. 

Roughly 20,000 men aged 26 and over would be exempted outright.

The reserve track could provide real manpower, but the blanket exemption would turn years of nonservice into a permanent release from the obligation.

Eisenkot wants both soldiers and ultra-Orthodox coalition partners. The reserve track is aimed at the first, the exemption at the second.
